TL;DR
Most "free" tool categories, margin audits, schema checkers, "see what your site is missing", keep your inputs. The price is paid in data, not dollars.
A 5-test browser audit takes under a minute and exposes the data flow before you type a single real number.
A 4-tier data model tells you what to share, where, and with whom: Public, Competitive-sensitive, Operational, Regulated.
Every tool on this site is held to a 9-claim standard, four of which are enforced as build invariants.

Most “free margin audit” tools have a price tag. It is just paid in data. The pattern is well-worn: you type your real ticket, your real food cost , your real labor, and the tool returns a number. It also tends to return sales reps in your inbox by morning, each with a proposal built on numbers that were never supposed to leave your office. The tool was the funnel . Your numbers were the qualifier.

The pattern hides because nobody asks the obvious question: where do my inputs go the moment I type them? In a working browser, you can answer that question in under a minute. This article is the framework, five tests, four data tiers, one worked example, and at the end, a checklist you can run on any tool you encounter.
The tools that pass these tests will tell you so, plainly. The tools that fail are about to explain why the tests do not apply to them. That is the tell.
1. The five tests, run before you type.
Open DevTools ↗ on whatever tool you are evaluating ( Cmd+Opt+I on Mac, Ctrl+Shift+I on Windows). Five questions:
Does typing a number trigger a network request? Open the Network tab. Type. If the request list grows on every keystroke, the tool is silently sending your inputs to a server. Walk away.
Is the privacy claim at the point of input? A trustworthy tool tells you what it does with your data where you are typing, not in a footer link three clicks deep.
Is there an account / newsletter / cookie gate? “Enter your email to see your results” means your numbers are the price of admission. The tool is not free.

Are there third-party analytics, session replay, or marketing scripts? Filter the Network tab by JS. If you see Google Analytics, Meta Pixel, HubSpot, FullStory, Hotjar, your inputs are being recorded by surveillance vendors who were not even part of the deal you thought you were making.
Is the source code readable? Right-click → View Source. A small, readable, unminified script is a tool you can audit. A 4-megabyte minified bundle from a SaaS framework is a tool you cannot.
Pass all five and the tool is at least honest about its data flow. Fail any of them and the tool either does not know or does not want you to know, both are reasons to leave.

The five-test browser audit, in the order you run them. Test one: open the Network tab and type a number. If a request fires on every keystroke, the tool is shipping your inputs to a server before you submit, walk away. Test two: look for the privacy claim at the point of input, not three clicks deep in a footer. Test three: check for an account, newsletter, or cookie gate, "enter your email to see your results" means your numbers are the price of admission. Test four: filter Network by JS and look for Google Analytics, Meta Pixel, HubSpot, FullStory, Hotjar, third-party surveillance vendors recording inputs you did not agree to share. Test five: right-click and View Source. A small, readable, unminified script is auditable; a four-megabyte minified bundle is not. Any single failure ends the audit.
2. The four-tier model, what to share, where.

Most small-business owners carry all their data in the same mental bucket, which means the supplier list and the tax ID get the same protection (often the same low level of it). Four tiers, each with a different audience and a different level of caution:
Tier 1, Public. Menu, hours, photos, address, phone, schema.org markup. Optimize aggressively; this is how customers find you.

Tier 2, Competitive-sensitive. Cost of goods, supplier list, your actual commission tier (not the public rate), labor schedule template. Share with bookkeeper / consultant / broker, under Nda. Not with platforms, competitors, or “free audit” tools that keep your input.
Tier 3, Operational-confidential. Monthly P&L, actual food cost %, customer pipeline, employee schedules. Inside the business only. P O S vendor, payroll, accountant, and only under written contract.

Tier 4, Regulated. Ssn, Ein, customer card data, bank details, food-safety logs, I-9s. Encrypted storage, access logging, contracts with cybersecurity terms. Never email. Never in a shared spreadsheet.

The principle: data never flows up a tier. A Tier 3 vendor does not get Tier 4 access just because they asked. A Tier 1 audience (a platform, a listing site) does not get Tier 2. The easiest way to reduce your attack surface is to stop volunteering data that was not actually required.

The four-tier data model, drawn as four rings sized by how widely each tier is allowed to travel. Tier one, public data like menu, hours, photos, and address, is fully open: optimize aggressively because this is how customers find you. Tier two, competitive-sensitive data like supplier list, real cost of goods, and the actual commission tier, flows only under Nda, shown as roughly three-quarters of the open circle. Tier three, operational-confidential data like the monthly P and L, food cost percentage, and customer pipeline, sits at about half: inside the business, only under written contract. Tier four, regulated data like Ssn, Ein, card data, and I-9s, is the smallest ring, encrypted-only, never email, never shared spreadsheets. The principle: data never flows up a tier.
3. What “safe” looks like, the worked example.

Here is the standard every tool on this site is held to. Nine claims about how every Muntin tool handles your inputs, each one verifiable in your own browser. Tap any claim to see the DevTools step that confirms it.
The 9 claims · expand for the proof
No fetch() , no XMLHttpRequest , no form submission fires when you type a financial number. Verify: open Network tab, type, watch for new entries. Should be zero.
The only endpoint a tool page uses is (code), the page itself. Verify: filter Network → Xhr/Fetch. Empty.
A 25 dollars ticket becomes 25-39 ; raw values are never event properties. Verify: filter Network → "plausible". Inspect the request body. No raw inputs.
Open Application → Storage. Tool inputs never persist there. Verify: type, then refresh. Inputs are gone, by design.
The only third-party script on a tool page is Plausible analytics, which only sees bucketed event names. Verify: filter Network → JS, look for unfamiliar origins. Should be empty.
The part after #, browsers never send fragments to servers, only the page before # . Verify: share a scenario link. Compare what is after the hash to what is in the request U R L Network shows.
No build step, no minification, every math function named. Verify: right-click → View Source. Read the script. If you cannot audit it, that is the failure mode.
Close the tab, reopen the tool. Empty form. No history, no recall. Verify: exactly that.
Print to P D F, no upload. Add to calendar, generates an .ics file locally, no A P I call. Verify: Network tab during the export action. Empty.

The full version with each claim's specific DevTools verification step lives at /security/ . Four of them (1, 2, 4, 5) are build invariants, the cohesion-check pass that runs on every deploy fails CI if a future tool ships a forbidden pattern. So “verifiable” is not marketing copy; it is a contract enforced by the build, with a public hash of the production bundle published at /security/integrity.txt .

A verdict tree for reading your DevTools results, where the failures are ordered by how serious they are. Start at the top. Did a network request fire on a keystroke, before you submitted anything? If yes, stop here and walk away, the tool is shipping your raw inputs to a server in real time, which is the most serious failure and overrides everything below it. If no, ask the next question: is there an account, email, or cookie gate between you and the result? If yes, the tool is not free; your numbers are the price of admission, so decline unless you would happily hand those numbers to the vendor's sales team. If no, ask whether third-party surveillance scripts like Meta Pixel, FullStory, or Hotjar are recording the page. If yes, treat it as a soft fail: the inputs may stay client-side, but the vendor invited watchers you never agreed to. If no third-party watchers, the last check is whether the source is readable and the privacy claim sits at the point of input. If both hold, the tool passes, it is at least honest about its data flow, the standard every Muntin tool is held to and enforces as a build invariant. The verdict pills read walk away in rust, not free and watched in amber, and safe to use in green.
"Verifiable" should be a build flag, not a marketing claim. If the only proof is the brochure, treat it as the brochure.
4. Run the audit.

The 5-test framework is also an interactive checklist at /learn/checklists/audit-any-tool/, walk through it with DevTools open on any tool you are evaluating. Save the result to your Workshop as a baseline; re-run it whenever a vendor pushes a “new feature.”

And if you find a tool that fails the audit but you cannot tell whether it is malicious or just sloppy, write through The Window and tell me about it. I read every one. The pattern of free tools that quietly turn operators into the product is worth naming, out loud, with the tool's name attached.
Key takeaways
Open DevTools, type, watch the Network tab. If a request fires per keystroke, walk away.
Privacy claims belong at the point of input, not three clicks deep in a footer.
Account / email / cookie gates mean the tool is not free. Your inputs are the price.
Data never flows up a tier. Tier 1 audiences never get Tier 2 data without a contract.
"Verifiable" should be a build flag, not a marketing claim.
Run the audit on a tool you are evaluating right now.

Open the tool you are thinking about using. Open DevTools. Walk through the five tests with the interactive checklist. Save the result to your Workshop as a baseline you can re-run when the vendor pushes a "new feature."
